unit.title: Respond to guest related complaints and requests

summary: This unit teaches housekeeping and villa staff to deal with what guests ask for and what goes wrong. You will learn to take, log and deliver guest requests, enter rooms correctly, listen to a complaint, show empathy, apologise, put right what you can, pass on what you cannot, keep records and follow up, so that the guest leaves satisfied and the property keeps its good name.

blocks.p: Guests judge a stay by how they are treated when they need something and when something goes wrong. A towel that arrives in five minutes, a bathroom that is put right with a smile, a member of staff who listens: these are remembered. A forgotten request or a shrug is remembered too, and today guests write about it online for thousands of people to read.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees, mainly in housekeeping, but the skills apply to every guest-facing job. You will meet requests (guests asking for something) and complaints (guests reporting a problem), and you must handle both politely, safely and with a record.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's mock room and lobby: role plays of three complaints with log entries and a work order, and delivering requests (including a Do Not Disturb room). The assessor watches your manner and safety as well as the paperwork.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical tasks use made-up guest names and details only. Keep the guest's details private even in a role play.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Requests and complaints: the difference and why they matter

head: Point
Request
Complaint
rows: What it is
The guest asks for something.
The guest reports a problem or is unhappy.
Examples
'Could I have two extra pillows?' 'Can I get an iron?'
'The bathroom is dirty.' 'The air conditioning does not cool.'
Your aim
Deliver quickly and correctly.
Listen, put it right, and win back the guest's trust.
Record
Request log
Complaint log (and a work order if it needs a repair)

blocks.p: A guest who has a problem and tells you gives you a chance to fix it. A guest who says nothing may simply leave and never return. So **welcome complaints**. A guest whose complaint is handled well is often more loyal than one who never had a problem, and tells others about the good service.

blocks.h: Why this matters to the property

ul: **Repeat guests:** happy guests come back. A **repeat guest** is one who stays again and again, and these guests are the most valuable.
**Reviews:** guests write comments and star ratings on travel websites. One bad review can be seen by thousands of people.
**Feedback:** the comments guests give, good or bad, show where the property can improve.
**Cost:** it is cheaper to fix a problem quickly than to give refunds, lose guests or pay for repairs after damage.

head: Person or place
Role
rows: Room attendant
Cleans and services rooms; first to hear many requests and complaints.
Supervisor
Checks rooms, solves what attendants cannot, can often approve gestures such as a free item.
Executive housekeeper
The manager in charge of the whole housekeeping department.
Maintenance (engineering)
Repairs fixtures such as taps, toilets, air conditioning and lights.
Security
Deals with safety, disturbances, theft and keys.
Front desk
Keeps guest records and room status; handles check-in, check-out, room moves and bills.
Linen room
The room on each floor where clean linen and guest supplies are stored.

blocks.note: Know the limit of your authority. Offering a refund, a discount or a free item is normally a decision for a supervisor or manager who has that authority. Do not promise one yourself.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Requests arrive by phone, by the front desk, or in person when a guest stops you in the corridor. Treat each one the same way: listen, confirm, log, deliver, close.

flow: Greet the guest politely and listen to the whole request
Confirm the room number, the items and how many
Ask if there is anything else, and about special needs
Say how soon you will deliver
Write it in the request log
Collect clean, correct items from the trolley or the linen room
Deliver: knock, announce, hand over or set up
Ask if anything else is needed, then close the request in the log with the time

blocks.p: The request log makes sure that a request is not forgotten and can be tracked. It is also the way the next shift sees what is still open.

head: Include
Why
rows: Room number
So the right guest gets the item.
The request, with quantities
'2 extra pillows, hypoallergenic' is clear; 'pillows' is not.
Time received
So response time can be checked.
Who took it and who delivered it
So there is someone to ask if something goes wrong.
Time delivered and closed
So it is clear the request is finished.

blocks.note: Deliver promptly, within the time the property sets. A guest who asks for an iron at 9 p.m. is likely to want it now. If you cannot deliver in the time you promised, phone the guest and say so.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Common requests and how to handle them

head: Request
How to handle it
rows: Extra towels, toilet paper, soap, shampoo
Take them from the trolley or linen room, never from another guest's room. Check they are clean.
Extra pillows or blankets
Ask about allergies. Bring clean pillows with fresh pillowcases.
Feather allergy
Remove feather pillows and duvets from the room and bring hypoallergenic pillows and bedding with fresh covers. Note it so the room is prepared for future stays.
Baby cot

Bring a clean cot. Set it up on a flat floor away from curtain cords, windows and lamps. Check it is steady and its sides are locked, and put nothing loose inside. Wash your hands before handling a clean cot.
Iron and ironing board
Check the iron works and the cable is undamaged. Set up the board on a flat floor away from the bed, with the cable out of walkways. Tell the guest to switch off the iron after use.
Something the property does not have
Explain politely and offer another choice, or suggest where they can get it.
Hair dryer, adaptor, extra hangers
Check it works; adaptors only if the property provides them.
Late turndown or room service tray removal
Log it and do it at the time agreed.

ul: **Allergies:** treat every allergy seriously. Check ingredients with the kitchen, or products with your supervisor. Never guess.
**Families with babies:** a cot, baby bath, extra towels, a bottle warmer if the property has one. Check safety.

**Older guests or guests with disabilities:** offer help with bags, a room near the lift, a chair in the bathroom, grab rails or a roll-in shower if the property has an accessible room. Ask, 'How can I help you best?'
**Medicine:** never give guests medicine. Direct them to the front desk or a doctor.

blocks.note: When you lift and carry items (a cot, an ironing board, a stack of linen) bend your knees, keep your back straight and ask for help if it is heavy. A back injury can end your career.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A guest room is the guest's private home for the stay. The way you enter, and what you do or do not say about it, protects the guest and the property.

blocks.h: Entering a room to deliver a request

flow: Check the door for a Do Not Disturb (DND) sign before you knock
Knock firmly three times and say 'Housekeeping'
Wait about ten seconds. If there is no answer, knock again and repeat
If still no answer, open the door slowly, announce again and look before you enter
If the guest is in, apologise and ask if now is a good time
Keep the door open while you work, and leave when done

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Door has a Do Not Disturb sign, but the guest asked for towels earlier
Do not knock. Phone the room, or report to the supervisor or front desk, as the property's rule says.
You go in and find the guest asleep
Leave quietly and come back later. Tell the supervisor and record it.
The guest is in the bathroom or dressing
Apologise, close the door quietly and wait outside.
A person in the corridor says it is their room and asks you to open it
Do not open it. They may not be the registered guest. Politely send them to the front desk, where their identity can be checked.
A guest asks which room a friend is in
Do not say. Refer her politely to the front desk.

blocks.note: Keep your master key or key card on you at all times, on a cord or clip. Never leave it in a door or on the trolley, and never lend it. Never say a guest's name or room number aloud where others can hear.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Do not touch, move, open or read the guest's belongings, papers, bags or phones.
Do not use the guest's phone, computer or toilet.
Do not take anything, even food or drink left in the room.
Report anything unusual (for example a person staying who is not on the booking) to your supervisor.

blocks.p: A guest who complains is often upset, tired or embarrassed. They want to be heard, to see you take it seriously and to see something done. Use the four steps **LAST**.

head: Letter
Step
What you do
rows: L
Listen
Stop what you are doing. Face the guest, make eye contact, nod. Do not interrupt. Let the guest finish.
A
Apologise
Say sorry sincerely, for example 'I am sorry, Mrs. Clarke. I will put this right now.' Do not blame anyone, make excuses or say 'it is not my fault'.
S
Solve
Put right what you can within your authority. If you cannot, say you will get your supervisor now. Tell the guest what will happen and when.
T
Thank
Thank the guest for telling you. It helped you to find and fix the problem.

blocks.p: **Empathy** means showing that you understand how the guest feels. You may not agree with everything, but you can say, 'I understand how frustrating that must be.' Empathy calms people. Sympathy ('Oh dear') is weaker; the guest wants understanding and action.

blocks.h: After listening: repeat the main points

blocks.p: Say, 'So the air conditioning has been noisy since last night and does not cool the room. Is that right?' This checks that you have understood, and it shows the guest you listened.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Face the guest and stand up straight
Turn away, look at your phone or the clock
Keep your arms relaxed and open
Fold your arms, point or put hands on hips
Make friendly eye contact and nod
Stare, or avoid looking at all
Speak in a calm, steady, polite voice
Raise your voice, sigh, or speak fast and sharply
Use the guest's title and surname: Mr., Mrs., Ms.
Use first names unless the guest asks you to
Stay calm even if the guest is angry
Take it personally or argue

blocks.note: Never argue with a guest who complains. Arguing makes it worse and solves nothing, even if the guest is wrong. Stay calm, listen, and get your supervisor if you cannot help.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Stay calm. Lower your own voice rather than raising it.
Let the guest finish.
Invite the guest to a quieter place, away from other guests, if the guest is willing.
Apologise and say what you will do, then do it.
If the guest becomes abusive or you feel unsafe, call your supervisor or security.

blocks.h: Telling the guest what will happen

blocks.p: Never say, 'I will see what I can do.' Say what will happen and when: 'I have called maintenance, and Mr. Brown will be at your room in 20 minutes.' If something takes longer, phone the guest to update them.

**Following up** means checking later that the guest is satisfied. Phone the room or speak to the guest the next day: 'I wanted to check that the air conditioning is working well now.' This shows you care, and it catches problems that were not fully fixed.

sections.title: Common complaints and what to do

blocks.p: Some complaints you can put right yourself. Others you must pass on. The table shows the usual response.

head: Complaint
What you do
Who deals with it
rows: Bathroom not clean; hair in the bath
Apologise at once
Ask if now is a good time, or come back while the guest is out
Re-clean the bathroom at once, with gloves and the right products
Replace towels and check
You, then tell the supervisor
Stained or dirty sheets or towels
Apologise
Remake the bed with fresh linen, and replace stained towels
You
Missing towels, soap, toilet paper
Apologise
Bring them from the trolley or linen room
You
Bin not emptied; dust seen
Apologise and fix it straight away
You
Noisy or non-cooling air conditioning; leaking tap; toilet that will not stop running; broken lock or light
Apologise
Report to maintenance on a work order
Tell the guest when it will be fixed and who will come
Offer another room if it cannot be fixed quickly
Maintenance; you report and follow up
Loud noise from another room, or a party
Apologise
Do not knock on the other guests' door yourself
Tell your supervisor or security
Security or supervisor
Rude staff member
Apologise and listen fully
Do not defend or blame the colleague
Report it to the supervisor
Supervisor
Brown or no water from the tap
Apologise
Offer bottled water
Report it to maintenance at once
Tell the guest when it is expected back
Maintenance and supervisor
Cockroaches, ants, mosquitoes in the room
Apologise and report at once
Offer a room move if it is serious
Never spray insecticide in the guest's presence without the property's approval
Supervisor and the pest-control contractor
Money or property missing
Take it seriously and stay calm
Do not accuse anyone, and do not search the room or luggage
Report to supervisor and security at once
Supervisor and security
Request delivered late
Apologise sincerely
Deliver now
Find out why, and stop it happening again
You and supervisor
A guest asks for a refund, discount or free item
Listen and apologise
Do not promise
Refer to the supervisor or manager
Supervisor or manager

blocks.note: Mosquitoes can spread dengue fever. Guests in Jamaica often complain about them, so report any standing water, clogged drains or buckets that hold water, and tell your supervisor if a guest asks for a net or a repellent.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Water lock-offs and power cuts happen in Jamaica. If a guest complains about no water or no light, apologise, say how long you expect it to take, offer bottled water or a torch, and tell your supervisor, who may arrange the tank, pump or generator.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Ants often come in a line to food left out in a guest room. Do not just wipe them away. Report the food source to your supervisor, clean the area, and tell the guest how to store food in sealed containers. Bed bugs hide in mattress seams and must be reported at once; do not strip or move the bed until your supervisor says so.

head: Situation
Do
Do not
rows: Strong smell of gas (for example from an LPG cooker)
Tell everyone to leave the room or villa
Open doors and windows if it is safe to do so
Report at once to the supervisor and call for help as the property's emergency plan says
Use flames, matches or lighters
Switch lights, fans or sockets on or off
Stay inside or investigate yourself
Guest says money or a watch is missing
Stay calm and say you are sorry this has happened
Report to supervisor and security at once
Write down exactly what the guest tells you, with time and room
Accuse anyone
Say the guest has lost it
Search the room or the luggage
Touch or move things
Loud party or disturbance
Apologise to the complaining guest
Tell the supervisor or security
Confront the noisy guests alone
A guest is hurt or ill
Stay with the guest
Call the supervisor and the first aider or emergency services at once
Give medicine
Move an injured guest unless there is danger
Guest finds a pest or insect
Apologise
Report
Offer a room move
Joke about it, or blame the guest
Fire, smoke or alarm
Follow the property's evacuation plan
Help guests leave by the exit
Use the lift
Go back for belongings

blocks.h: Using chemicals to put a complaint right

ul: Read the label, and the safety data sheet (SDS), before you use any cleaning product.
Measure the dilution exactly. Wear gloves, and eye protection when the label says.
**Never mix bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners.** They give off a poisonous gas.
Keep the bathroom aired: open the window or put on the extractor fan.
Put out a **wet floor sign** after mopping, and wipe up spills at once.
Keep chemicals on the lower shelf of the trolley, away from clean linen, in labelled containers.

blocks.note: A guest should never be left in a room full of chemical fumes. Ask the guest if they would like to step out while you clean.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Why complaints and requests are recorded

ul: So nothing is forgotten, and the next shift can see what is still open.
So supervisors can see how quickly the team responds.
So repeated problems can be found and fixed at the root: for example, many guests complain about the same room's air conditioner.
So the property can show what happened and when, if a guest later disputes it.

head: Record
What it contains
rows: Complaint log
Date and time; guest name and room; the problem; the action taken; who dealt with it; outcome; follow-up and guest's response.
Request log
Room; request; time received; who took it; who delivered; time closed.
Work order
A form sent to maintenance asking for a repair: room, fault, date and time, urgency, your name; later the repair details.
Lost property log
Item found, where, when, by whom, and who it was handed to.

blocks.p: Records must be **clear, accurate and factual**. Write what happened, not your opinion. Do not write rude or personal comments about the guest. Keep records private and out of guests' sight.
**Escalation** means passing a complaint up to a supervisor or manager to deal with. Do it when:

ul: you cannot put it right yourself, or it is outside your job (a repair, a refund, a room move);
it is serious (safety, theft, a health problem);
the guest asks for a manager;
the guest is still unhappy after you have done your best.

blocks.p: Tell the guest, 'I will get my supervisor now,' and stay with the guest until the supervisor arrives, if you can. Give the supervisor the facts, so the guest does not have to repeat the whole story.

ul: Anything you find in a checked-out room, such as a gold ring under the bed or a phone charger, is **handed in to lost property** and recorded. Do not keep it, even if it seems small.
In an occupied room, leave guests' things where they are, and dust round them.

blocks.h: Handover at the end of the shift

blocks.p: At the end of your shift, write any requests and complaints that are still open in the log and hand them over to the next shift in person. An open complaint that is not handed over is a forgotten complaint.

blocks.note: Complimentary means free. A complimentary item or an upgrade is a gift from the property. Only a person with authority can give one. Do not offer a complimentary item unless your supervisor has told you that you may.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain the difference between a guest request and a complaint, and why both are welcome
take a request by phone or in person: listen, confirm, say how soon, log it and close it
write a complete entry in the request log and a complaint log
deliver clean, safe items, including a cot, an iron and hypoallergenic pillows
enter a room correctly, respect a Do Not Disturb sign and deal with a sleeping guest
refuse politely to open a room for a stranger, and not give out a room number
use LAST: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank
show empathy and use calm body language and voice
repeat a complaint back to check I have understood it
tell which complaints I can put right and which I must pass on
respond safely to a gas smell, missing money, noise, pests and brown water
use cleaning chemicals safely when I re-clean
complete a work order for a repair
escalate a complaint to my supervisor and stay with the guest
hand in found property and hand over open items at the end of my shift
follow up to check the guest is satisfied

c1.title: A dirty bathroom at a Negril villa
c1.text: Mrs. Samuels, a guest at a villa in Negril, stops room attendant Shanice in the corridor at 2 p.m. She says, 'I came back from the beach and the bathroom is a disgrace. There is hair in the shower and a stained towel.' She is upset and her voice is rising. Shanice cleaned the room that morning but was in a hurry because two early arrivals were waiting.

c2.title: Noise at night in Ocho Rios
c2.text: At 11:30 p.m., Mr. and Mrs. Campbell phone the front desk to say loud music is coming from the villa next door and they cannot sleep. Night supervisor Orane receives the call. The Campbells are repeat guests who have stayed three times. Room attendant Nadine is also on shift, but her job is housekeeping, not security.

c3.title: Requests from the Dixon family
c3.text: The Dixon family are staying in a villa in Mandeville. Mrs. Dixon phones the housekeeping desk and asks for a baby cot and for two pillows without feathers, as her husband is allergic. She adds that they are going out soon. Later, trainee Tyrone is sent to deliver the pillows but finds a Do Not Disturb sign on the door. Earlier that afternoon, he knocked at a different villa, got no answer, entered and found a guest asleep.

c4.title: Missing money and a found ring
c4.text: Mr. Chambers, a guest at a Kingston hotel, reports that J$20,000 and a watch are missing from his room. He is angry and says, 'It must be the cleaners.' Later that day, room attendant Kerry-Ann is cleaning a checked-out room and finds a gold ring under the bed. A man in the corridor tells her he left something in room 118 and asks her to let him in.

c5.title: Maintenance problems at a Treasure Beach villa
c5.text: At a guest villa in Treasure Beach, a guest reports a strong smell of gas from the kitchen. A second guest says the air conditioning in his bedroom has been noisy and not cooling since last night. A third guest says the tap water is brown. The villa manager is away, and room attendant Marlon is the only member of staff on site.

c6.title: A rude remark and the end of the shift
c6.text: Mrs. Powell, a guest in a Montego Bay hotel, complains that a room attendant was rude to her this morning. She asks for a free night as compensation. Supervisor Mrs. Rowe is on break. Later, room attendant Odane is about to go off shift with two requests and one complaint still open in his log.

questions.q: Mrs. Samuels is upset and talking quickly. What should Shanice do first?
o: Tell her that the room was cleaned properly that morning
Stop what she is doing and listen to the whole complaint
Offer her a free drink at the bar to calm her down
Go and check the bathroom before saying anything to her
questions.why: The first step is to listen, face the guest and let her finish. Defending yourself, offering a gift or walking away before she has been heard makes an upset guest angrier.

questions.q: Which response best shows empathy and a sincere apology?
o: Sorry about that, but it is a very busy day for all of us here
I will see what I can do about it later on this afternoon
I am sorry, Mrs. Samuels. I understand. I will put it right now.
That is strange, because I know very well that I cleaned it this morning
questions.why: A good apology recognises the guest's feelings, takes responsibility without excuses and says what will happen now. Excuses, vague promises and doubting the guest are all poor responses.

questions.q: How should Shanice deal with the bathroom itself?
o: Ask the next shift to clean it, as she is busy with the arrivals
Ask when it suits Mrs. Samuels, then re-clean it and replace the towel
Give the guest some cleaning cloths so that she can wipe it herself
Re-clean it while Mrs. Samuels is standing in the bathroom, to save time
questions.why: A cleaning fault in her own job is hers to put right straight away, at a time that suits the guest. She should replace the stained towel too, and tell her supervisor.

questions.q: What should Orane do about the noise complaint?
o: Apologise to the Campbells and send security or the supervisor
Tell the Campbells that parties are all part of a holiday in Jamaica
Phone the villa next door and tell the guests to stop the music at once
Ask Nadine to knock on the next villa's door and tell them to be quiet
questions.why: Noise from other guests is handled by security or the supervisor, not by housekeeping alone. Orane should apologise, act quickly and keep the Campbells informed.

questions.q: The Campbells are repeat guests. What is the best way to treat this complaint?
o: Treat it like any other and do only what the log requires of the staff
Give them a free night straight away to keep their loyalty to the villa
Handle it quickly and carefully, as they are valued returning guests
Tell them that other guests have complained about the noise before them
questions.why: Every guest deserves the same quick, polite response, and repeat guests are especially valuable. Promising a free night is not the attendant's decision, and revealing information about other guests is wrong.

questions.q: What should Orane do the next morning?
o: Nothing, as the matter was dealt with last night
Record it in the log, and follow up with the Campbells
Ask the Campbells to write a letter of complaint first
Delete the log entry, to keep the property's record clean
questions.why: Records and follow-up are part of the job. Orane should log the complaint and check that the Campbells are now satisfied. Hiding complaints stops the property from learning and fixing repeated problems.

questions.q: What should Tyrone check after setting up the baby cot?
o: The sides are locked, the cot is steady and nothing is loose in it
The cot has two soft pillows and a thick blanket for the baby's comfort
The cot stands right beside the window so that the baby gets fresh air
The cot is the same height as the parents' bed that is in the room
questions.why: A cot must be clean, steady, with its sides locked, and without pillows or loose bedding. It should be away from windows, cords and lamps.

questions.q: Which pillows should Tyrone bring for Mr. Dixon?
o: Feather pillows in fresh covers
Any pillows, as the covers are what matter
Two hypoallergenic pillows with fresh pillowcases
Foam pillows taken from a spare room, in the same covers
questions.why: Hypoallergenic pillows do not contain feathers. Fresh covers help too. Pillows from another room might have been used or might contain feathers.

questions.q: Tyrone finds a Do Not Disturb sign on the Dixons' door. What should he do?
o: Phone the room or ask the supervisor, rather than knock
Knock once, quietly, in case the guests did not mean it
Leave the pillows outside the door without telling anyone
Open the door with his key and put them on the bed
questions.why: A Do Not Disturb sign means do not knock or enter. Phone the room, or follow the property's rule, to deliver the request without disturbing the guests.

questions.q: Earlier, Tyrone entered a villa after announcing himself and found the guest asleep. What should he have done?
o: Wake the guest gently, apologise and offer to clean now
Stay and clean quietly, as he has a time target to meet
Leave quietly and come back later, and tell the supervisor
Close the curtains and switch on the fan to make the guest comfortable
questions.why: A sleeping guest must not be disturbed. Leave quietly, return later and record it. Doing any work, or adjusting things in the room, could wake the guest.

questions.q: Mr. Chambers says it must be the cleaners. What should Kerry-Ann do?
o: Tell him that room attendants never steal from guests, so it must be lost
Say sorry, report to security and the supervisor, and accuse no one
Search the room herself to see whether the money is hidden somewhere
Ask him how much money he had and why he did not use the room safe
questions.why: Take the guest seriously, stay calm, and report at once to the supervisor and security. Do not accuse, search or touch anything, because security may need to see the room as it is.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do with the gold ring she found?
o: Keep it safe in her pocket in case the guest phones
Hand it to lost property and record it
Leave it on the pillow for the next guest
Give it to the first guest who says it is theirs
questions.why: Found items are handed in to lost property and recorded. They are never kept, left behind or given out without the guest proving ownership.

questions.q: The man in the corridor says he left something in room 118 and asks Kerry-Ann to open it. What should she say?
o: Ask him what the item is, and open the door if he can describe it
Open the door, as he is only going in to take his own belongings
Say that she will go and look for it herself and bring it to him
Politely send him to the front desk to have his identity checked
questions.why: A person who says he is the guest may not be. Only the front desk can check who the guest is and arrange access. Kerry-Ann should be polite and never open the room herself.

questions.q: Marlon asks the guests to leave the villa kitchen area while the gas smell is checked. Why?
o: The smell may spoil their food and make them feel unwell later
Gas can build up and ignite, or harm anyone who breathes it
The maintenance team cannot work while guests are in the room
The guests might use their phones and spoil the leak report
questions.why: Leaking gas can catch fire or explode from a small spark and can make people ill, so the first aim is to get people away and call for help. Switches and flames must not be used.

questions.q: What should Marlon do about the air conditioning that is noisy and does not cool?
o: Tell the guest to open the windows and the problem will go away
Switch the unit off and say nothing, as it may be dangerous to use
Open the cover and try to fix it herself with a screwdriver
Apologise, fill in a work order and say when it will be repaired
questions.why: Repairs go to maintenance on a work order. Marlon should apologise, say when and who will come, and offer another room if it cannot be fixed quickly. He should not repair it himself.

questions.q: A guest says the tap water is brown. What is the best thing for Marlon to do for her immediately?
o: Apologise and offer bottled water while he reports it
Tell her the water is safe to drink if she lets it run clear
Tell her that this happens often after a water lock-off
Ask her to have a bath in the other bathroom instead
questions.why: Offer a safe alternative straight away, apologise and report the problem so it can be checked and fixed. Do not tell guests that water of doubtful quality is safe.

questions.q: After the air conditioning is repaired, what should Marlon do to finish the complaint?
o: Close the work order and make no further contact with the guest about it
Check with the guest that the room is cool, and complete the log
Wait for the guest to say that the problem has been fixed again
Offer the guest a free night as a reward for being so patient with us
questions.why: Following up shows care and catches repairs that did not work. The log should record the outcome. A free night is not Marlon's decision.

questions.q: Mrs. Powell asks for a free night. Who can give one?
o: Any member of staff, if the guest has a good reason
The room attendant, if she says sorry in person
The receptionist, as part of check-out
A supervisor or manager who has that authority
questions.why: Compensation such as a free night is a decision for a person with authority. The attendant should listen, apologise, report it and not promise anything.

questions.q: Mrs. Powell says a room attendant was rude. How should Odane respond?
o: Apologise and listen, and report it to the supervisor
Explain that the attendant is new and was having a bad day
Tell her that he did not see it and so cannot do anything
Ask her to describe what the attendant looks like so she can be punished
questions.why: Listen fully, apologise and pass it on. Do not defend or blame the colleague. The supervisor investigates.

questions.q: What should Odane do with his open requests and complaint at the end of his shift?
o: Leave them in the log, as the next person will see them
Finish them after his shift ends, without telling anyone
Hand them over in the log to the next shift, in person
Tear out the pages so that the next shift starts clean
questions.why: Open items must be handed over, in the log and in person, so they are finished. An open complaint that nobody knows about is a forgotten complaint.
